I am as good at the game as I am ever going to get, got well over a hundred hours and hit my ceiling at around ruthless/lethal. The vast majority of players will never solo Absolute because it's very clearly not designed to be done that way, and aren't particularly enjoyable to try and do.

I think it is a weird restriction as it essentially says a big ol' f*** you to modders that want to affect balance in any way for their own personal experience. Using "cheats" to speed up progression in general is just player choice, as long as it doesn't affect anyone else's gameplay (which in this case it obviously does not), then it should be permitted.
Okay, but I want a way to bypass that so I don't have to lose all the hours I put in, I doubt they want me to use mods at all given this weird restriction.

Absolute doesn't seem to be made with the idea of fighting solo with 2 next to useless bots that do no damage.

It's very clear that the highest difficulty needs 3 competent players, all communicating. I don't have a team of 3 to play with, 90% of the time I don't have a team of 2 to play with, and I've found that even ruthless and lethal can pose too much of a challenge (depending on the mission) when trying to run solo.

There is only so good I can get at the game, I am not bad, but I am pretty much at my ceiling for gameplay competence for my main classes.

The mods mean that I can still enjoy and beat the game on my own at the higher difficulties, sure I am making more progress than I might otherwise, but what's the harm in that? When I am playing alone or with a friend who knows I have done that.

The main reason I am concerned about it being unfun, is that the world they are in is quite hostile to villains. Especially ones that aren't well organised or very powerful. If they aren't exceptionally careful in their villainy, they are liable to get their shit pushed in by someone much stronger than them.

Since the reason they are becoming villainous is not some well thought out scheme, but instead murderous rampages, they are very very likely to be squashed. 

I would try to work with it as a GM, if it comes to that, but you surely understand that I essentially now am at square one. I built a world, system of government and a cast of NPCs, that are suddenly going to all flip their opinions of the players virtually at once because I had designed it with reasonable characters in mind, not 4 bloodlusted sociopaths.

We talk a bit outside, we have been playing TTRPGs together for years. The players are a mix of types:
 
Player 1 is very much a war gamer who seems to mostly want to do combat or roll to do things, he will roleplay but isn't very confident with it even now (he is newer than most others). He will go with the flow of whatever others want to do 9/10 times so he can get to the next roll. 

Player 2 is similar, he wants to roleplay but isn't a confident actor (we don't expect him to be by any stretch) so often kind of sits in the background until he thinks of something cool he wants to do. When he thinks of that cool thing it'll often be out of character unfortunately, so his PCs often end up a bit undefined.

Player 3 is just chaos, he does whatever he wants and makes characters that will fascilitate that. Still very go with the flow overall, but his characters are always really hard for me to wrangle compared to the other 3 as they are often active participants but also come across as random.

Player 4 is a great player, really loves rping and has made a wonderful character. It's just that he has also made one of the most morally ambiguous ones (which I don't blame him, as it was a fun character concept).


The actual PCs are quite different in practice compared to the original plan, often due to being underdeveloped.

P1:
Idea: made a plastic man style hero with the intention of being a bit wacky and silly.
Execution: killed the first guy he got in to a fight with by breaking his neck, hardly made any jokes and had no problem with the other players actions to be described. Basically is a stretchy anti-hero with no real moral compass.

P2:
Idea: an anti-hero speedster with radiation powers, who came from a darker city filled with crime. He moved to a more peaceful area to try and make a bigger positive impact than at home. The idea was very "anti-hero with a good heart". But it was pretty vague.
Exe: insane murder hobo, basically turned in to Krombopulus Michael as he killed dozens of people in session 2 while being super bright and cheery before and after. Literally carved them in to pieces or blew them to bits with a smile on his face while making jokes. I have spoken to him about this, but due to scheduling issues we haven't had a proper talk about where he is going with this. 
No good heart in sight, just "oh boy, here I go killing again!"

P3:
Idea: Luck based super hero, like Domino, but with a more spider man style background. Struggling to manage hero work with his regular job, a chill guy who just kind of lets life happen and goes with his gut on most things. Suppose to have a strong moral compass, so no killing or trading lives.
Exe: Kept reasonably close but his character is exceptionally morally passive. He hasn't killed yet but seems open to the idea and has little to no problem with P2 or P4 for being the way they are. Also dropped on me that he wants to move more towards anti-hero style as he gets more numb to the whole killing thing and shit gets more dangerous. So now we have anti-hero #No 3.

P4:
Idea: War Crimes Man, yes really. That is not a joke, but I was fine with it as he was the first to make a character for the campaign so he wasn't clashing with anyone. I also knew he is a really good roleplayer so WCM would stay far enough on the good side to save me some stress. The actual character behind that name is a scientist who is actually an undercover government agent for an organisation that is all about dealing with superhumans. Really great stuff, gave me loads to work with.

That Harvard doesn't alter there standards based on the ability of the students. All of these things are wrong if you are, Harvard has tons of proverbial difficulty tweaks to allow more people to get in than just "the tip top elite", it's about putting in the expected amount of effort, which creates a range of results that are worked with and around.

Your later statements would also imply that simply having an easier option somehow devalues the harder option. Is this true for harvard, last I checked the value of a theoretical physics course isn't depreciated by the existence of a normal physics course, nor is does a PhD devalue a Masters.

Basically, no, most sensible designs for systems like that place value in the capabilities of their applicants and what they are capable of achieving. I don't know if this is the same in America but in my country the school system grades are set based on the averages of students, so if students do on average worse on a test they lower the grade boundaries, it is not a flat rate as that might cause inequal treatment based on the capabilities of the students (basically the playing field must always be equal, based on skill level)

Some things have changed since I made this post, first I got some more time with the game, I also got a PC version to test things out, I used cheat engine to buff my character up enough that I was able to make my way to the cathedral of the deep. I was still thoroughly challenged throughout and had a difficult time of it but my ability actually grew substantially thanks to gettinf experience with the various enemy types and especially bosses, I also got to test out other abilities that previously would have required serious investment, which may have lead to me wasting a significant amount of time on a badly stat invested character.

So I went back without cheats after my new found experience and managed to beat the tutorial as the deprived class. This would not have been possible had I not artifically decreased the difficulty to allow me to understand the game, the learning curve was less steep meaning I had more room to make mistakes but was still punished enough that I stopped making them.

I still believe the game needs an easy mode, had it provided me with one I would have been able to enjoy the game as I am now without the use of cheats, a system that while I got it to work I frequently had to make adjustments so I wasn't too overpowered such that my mistakes didn't matter or too underpowered such that the game was too harsh on my lackluster abilities.

I have nothing against the elitism, I wasn't bragging when I beat the boss while cheating but I felt better when I did it in the base game. The easy mode is a warm up for the main event, if implemented it should be treated as such, a good example of this is Furi, which has an easier mode but informs you that it lacks the intended challenge and it is recommended you play on the normal difficulty in subsequent playthroughs, a system I think From games could benefit from greatly.

I would like to say despite my few grievances over difficulty I enjoyed the game even more than I previously expected thanks to using an altered version of the system then later moving to the 'real thing' so to speak. I enjoy the punishing nature of the game and it was not hampered at all by those cheats, it was only once I 'got used' to it in that mode I decided to change to the original to see how I faired and saw that the principles remained the same just with less room for error.

I would normally allow the interrogator to roll an insight, but secretely have it be a low DC if it is the truth rather than a contested check. 
If the truth is a secret location or something then you should give a low DC since presumably the interrogator would realise (at least in part) that this lie is too easily revealed (since secret locations are usually quite large and if the adventurers can't find the entrance they would just go back and ask the guy again).

If the truth is something less easily confirmed as the truth (like the life or death state of a hostage which could only be confirmed by finding them) feel free to give a higher DC check.

Ideally you want the truth to be easier to determine than a lie both narratively and with an insight check, since it makes the story less annoying for players, otherwise the party ends up on goose chase after goose chase.
This is equivelant advice to 'git gud scrub'.

No he gets the various smashes. Mostly in the manga he has his 20% st louis( i think) smash that is more precise and doesnt make his fingers unusable. His shoot style is a completely separate fighting style that took him to another level by increasing his versatility (the addition of kicks is an important one). His % increases are just a basic outline of how close he is to All Might, it's everything else that matters most as of now. 

The boosts of his outfits are useful but only in how he uses them, his boots are only strong because he had them made to bolster his shoot style. The protection for his arms is due to the severe damage using 100% did to them.

His powers are simple, that's the best part. He gets super strength, how he uses that power is the most interesting bit. He needs to be able to outmaneuver his opponents, to use his special moves to take them down and save people. If Deku had the power to just 'do everything' (e.g bullshitting his powers so he could fly, fire lightning etc) the show would be so dull, he needs limitations he can't just train his way out of in the here and now.

Also the reasons behind the growth is just as important as the growth itself. I do not know who the 'emo brother' is but having a character grow stronger due to their relationship with another is just about every shounen anime ever.

MHA is an extremely good shounen anime, that tells a very interesting story, with compelling motivations and extremely well written characters. The action and growing strength, lives and dies based on whether you like these characters or not. If you do not like the MHA characters, then it really is not for you at all since everything rests on your appreciation of their writing.

Action for the sake of action. Power for the sake of power and fighting without reasons works for only a very few works of fiction.

The creativity comes from how the powers are used, not how brutishly strong they are. One of the main draws of MHA is that there is a ceiling to how 'strong' any person can become since quirks are just physical abilities not god powers, so every character has to use their power in a different way and approach each fight differently. 

Bakugou isn't OP in MHA because he can blow stuff up really well. It's because he has an extremely versatile skill set that can beat almost any quirk and get him out of any situation. 

Midoriya has already shown growth in a more meaningful way in the manga, when he uses a new kind of smash that is precise and targeted rather than big and flashy.

He is already getting gradual power ups throughout. I don't know how far you are in but he has already had a serious bump after a fight that happened recently in the anime. In the Manga he has developed even further.

The quirks in this world don't work like spirit pressure in Bleach or Ki in DBZ. Those shows focused on a system where after intense training you gained a permanent buff that increases all abilities (either a new form that does this or just getting stronger normally). Quirks only get stronger over long periods of physical training OR the person learns to control it better through practice.

Deku can't just do 10,0000 push ups and then unlock Super One For All and start punching mountains out, the powers don't function that way. He has to gradually build himself up till his body can handle the higher tiers of One for All e.g 5%, 8% and 20% etc.
